name: StimBank Electrical Brain Stimulation Database (Harmonized Clinical Taxonomy)

Sensory.desc: Responses include auditory, visual, gustatory, olfactory, vestibular, body perception, and somatosensory

subdomains.name: Auditory
subdomains.desc: Evoked simple perceptions (ringing, water running, mumbling, buzzing, whistle), complex perceptions (voices, music), or auditory illusions (pitch change, sounds louder, ear obstruction, sound distortion).

response_type_definitions.Auditory Simple: Evoked simple auditory perceptions such as ringing, water running, mumbling, buzzing, ringing, whistle
response_type_definitions.Auditory Complex: Evoked complex auditory perceptions such as voices with clear or unclear content, or music
response_type_definitions.Auditory Illusions: Alterations in auditory perception such as sounds appearing louder, sensation of ear obstruction, change in pitch, echo, or sound distortion.

subdomains.name: Visual
subdomains.desc: Evoked simple perceptions (phosphenes, flashes, shadows, shapes, moving dots), complex perceptions (faces, characters, scenes, cartoons), or visual illusions (halo, metamorphopsia, micropsia/macropsia, visual motion).

response_type_definitions.Visual Simple: Evoked simple visual perceptions such as phosphenes, flashes, shadows, simple shapes, colors, moving or flickering lights/dots.
response_type_definitions.Visual Complex: Evoked complex visual perceptions such as faces or face parts, characters, animals, complex scenes, or cartoons
response_type_definitions.Visual Illusions: Alterations in visual perception such as changes in brightness/halo, face/letter/number distortions, changes in visual texture, illusion of visual motion, objects appearing smaller/larger (micropsia/macropsia).

subdomains.name: Gustatory
subdomains.desc: Identifiable or non-identifiable gustatory (taste), further classified by pleasant or unpleasant hedonic valence.

response_type_definitions.Pleasant: Taste experiences perceived as enjoyable, appetitive, or pleasant in hedonic tone.
response_type_definitions.Unpleasant: Taste experiences perceived as aversive, bitter, foul, or unpleasant in hedonic tone.

subdomains.name: Olfactory
subdomains.desc: Evoked olfactory (smell) perceptions, which can be identifiable or non-identifiable, and may have pleasant or unpleasant hedonic valence.

subdomains.name: Vestibular
subdomains.desc: Simple sensations of dizziness or vertigo, as well as complex whole-body displacement, graviceptive experiences (falling, floating, levitation), or rotation.

subdomains.name: Body Perception
subdomains.desc: Disturbances of body schema or image, such as out-of-body experiences, alien limb sensations, limb loss sensations, limb appearing to move, autoscopic and heautoscopic phenomena.

subdomains.name: Somatosensory
subdomains.desc: Somatosensory responses mapped by body part (upper limb, lower limb, head/neck/trunk) and classified as painful (burning, pinprick, muscle pain) or non-painful (tingling, thermal warmth, numbness, vibration, pressure).

response_type_definitions.Non-Painful: Somatosensory sensations such as tingling, warmth, numbness, pressure, or vibration without pain.
response_type_definitions.Painful: Painful somatosensory responses including burning, pricking, sharp, or aching sensations.
response_type_definitions.Upper Limb: Somatosensory responses localized to the upper limb, arm, hand, or fingers.
response_type_definitions.Lower Limb: Somatosensory responses localized to the lower limb, leg, foot, or hip.
response_type_definitions.Head/Neck/Trunk: Somatosensory responses localized to the head, neck, or trunk region.

Motor.desc: Primary, supplementary, and subcortical motor circuits controlling voluntary muscle contractions, eye movements, tremor regulation, and motor inhibition.

subdomains.name: Positive
subdomains.desc: Positive motor responses were defined as any evoked movement (indicated by terms such as movement, contraction, myoclonic, tonic, clonic, lifting, flexion, pronation, twitching, jerk, tremor, shaking). Further classified by effector, including upper limb (shoulder, arm, hand, fingers), lower limb (hip, leg, foot), head/neck/trunk, articulatory (tongue, lips, jaw, larynx), and/or eyes.

response_type_definitions.Upper limb: Movement responses involving the shoulder, arm, hand, or fingers.
response_type_definitions.Lower limb: Movement responses involving the leg, foot, or hip.
response_type_definitions.Head/neck/trunk: Movement responses involving the neck, trunk, or head musculature.
response_type_definitions.Articulatory: Motor responses affecting speech-related muscles such as tongue, lips, jaw, or larynx.
response_type_definitions.Eyes: Eye movement responses including saccades, conjugate eye deviation, or oculomotor effects.

subdomains.name: Negative
subdomains.desc: Negative responses were defined as arrest, disturbance, or slowing of movements. Further classified including upper limb (shoulder, arm, hand, fingers), lower limb (hip, leg, foot), head/neck/trunk, articulatory (tongue, lips, jaw, larynx), and/or eyes.

response_type_definitions.Upper limb: Movement arrest or interference affecting the arm, hand, or shoulder.
response_type_definitions.Lower limb: Movement arrest or interference affecting the leg, foot, or hip.
response_type_definitions.Head/neck/trunk: Movement arrest or interference affecting the neck, trunk, or head.
response_type_definitions.Articulatory: Speech or facial motor impairment involving tongue, lips, jaw, or laryngeal movements.
response_type_definitions.Eyes: Eye movement interruption or directional gaze suppression.

subdomains.name: Automatisms
subdomains.desc: Automatisms such as laughter without merriment or mirth, grasping, rubbing, vocalizations (excluding simple motor phenomena), yawning, chewing/mastication, oro-alimentary automatisms.

Cognitive.desc: Higher-order associative networks including language processing, speech arrest, naming anomia, experiential memory retrieval, and Theory of Mind.

subdomains.name: Language disturbances
subdomains.desc: Disruptions in language production, comprehension or written language.

response_type_definitions.Production: Impairment or alteration in language production, including complete interruption of speech or errors affecting the production of words and sentences.
response_type_definitions.Comprehension: Impairment in understanding or accessing the meaning of verbal information, including words and sentences (e.g., word comprehension deficits, auditory comprehension impairment, or lexico-semantic interference)
response_type_definitions.Written Language: Reading impairment/alexia (letters, words, or sentences) and writing impairment (e.g., agraphia or paragraphia).

subdomains.name: Derealization / Depersonalization
subdomains.desc: Feelings of derealization or depersonalization, such as feeling detached from the world or inside a dream, or feeling of going into a trance.

subdomains.name: Reminiscence/Déjà rêvé
subdomains.desc: Evoked visual, auditory, or multimodal complex perceptions accompanied by a subjective feeling of remembering or reexperiencing (e.g., flashbacks, recollection of a dream).

subdomains.name: Déjà vu/Déjà vécu/Jamais vu
subdomains.desc: Erroneous feelings of familiarity (déjà vu/déjà vécu) or unfamiliarity (jamais vu) for the current situation. Contrary to reminiscences and déjà rêvé, these phenomena are devoid of perceptual content.

subdomains.name: Other Focal Cognitive Changes
subdomains.desc: Focal cognitive changes, which included for example dyscalculia, working memory deficits, music processing disruptions, face recognition/discrimination deficits, or emotion recognition deficits.

Affective.desc: Evoked emotional experiences or changes in emotional state.

subdomains.name: Positive valence responses
subdomains.desc: Positive changes in affect

response_type_definitions.Happiness/Wellbeing: Positive affective changes associated with contentment, well-being, or pleasant mood.
response_type_definitions.Ecstatic/Bliss: Intense positive affect characterized by profound bliss, euphoria, or heightened wellbeing.
response_type_definitions.Mirth: Amusement or laughter-like affective responses without a necessarily broad emotional context.

subdomains.name: Negative valence responses
subdomains.desc: Negative changes in affect

response_type_definitions.Anger: Negative affective responses characterized by irritability, anger, or hostile emotional arousal.
response_type_definitions.Anxiety: Anxious or apprehensive emotional states, often with worry or tension.
response_type_definitions.Fear: Fearful affective states including panic, dread, or apprehension of threat.
response_type_definitions.Sadness: Negative affective states involving sadness, despair, or emotional dysphoria.

Autonomic.desc: Central autonomic network regulating visceral interoception, cardiac rhythm, vasomotor tone, and neurovegetative reflexes.

subdomains.name: Cardiovascular responses
subdomains.desc: Change in heart rate (subjective or objectively measured) or changes in blood pressure.

subdomains.name: Temperature responses
subdomains.desc: General sensations of cold or warmth (e.g. being cold, being warm, heat wave sensation, flushing, sweating).

subdomains.name: Visceral responses
subdomains.desc: Sudden facial flushing, skin sensation of extreme heat or localized vasoconstriction and sudden chill.

subdomains.name: Pupillary responses
subdomains.desc: Pupillary responses.

subdomains.name: Respiratory responses
subdomains.desc: Responses such as hypoventilation/apnea, hyperventilation/shortness of breath, or hypoxemia.

Agency.desc: Changes in the sense of agency, characterized by feeling that thoughts or actions are not self-generated or under one’s control, experiencing an urge to act, forced thinking, or sensing resistance to a planned action.

Consciousness.desc: Responses classified as altered consciousness/awareness included loss of consciousness or impaired awareness, unconscious movements (i.e., movements occurring without awareness), or the erroneous impression of having spoken out loud.

No Effect.desc: Stimulations explicitly reported as not evoking any functional response; absence of a specific response type without indication of whether other responses occurred was insufficient. This category was deliberately conservative to provide true non-response controls.

Other/ unclassifiable responses.desc: Stimulation responses that could not be assigned to any other domain. Examples include stimulation effects that could span several categories such as a “visceral/somatic response”, as well as unclear responses such as an “unpleasant sensation”, or rare specific responses that did not fall into any of the other domains.

sites.effect: <The stimulation elicited a smile starting from the contralateral zygomaticus muscle and subsequently involving all the lower facial muscles, without interrupting the speech. The facial expression was not accompanied by vocalization or any postural movement, resulting in a smile and not a laughter. Smile production was not accompanied by mirth and, more interestingly, the patient did not became aware that she produced a facial expression. More specifically, she did not spontaneously commented on her facial expression and, when explicitly asked whether she smiled, she responded negatively, stating that the stimulation was completely ineffective.>

sites.effect: <The high frequency stimulation of the adjacent contacts and gave similar results. During the stimulation, the patient exhibited an evident smile (latency ≅4 s) preserved after the end of the stimulation. No vocalizations accompanied the facial expression. The expression recovered suddenly and completely as the patient started to speak and answered questions. She reported only a very faint sensation behind the left ear and, when the neurologist explicitly asked whether she felt anything to the face, to the tongue or to the throat, the patient gave a negative answer.>

sites.effect: <One second after the stimulation onset the patient interrupted her speech (anarthria) and smiled. Similar to Patients 1, the facial expression was not accompanied by vocalization or any postural movement, resulting in a smile and not a laughter. When explicitly asked by the neurologist why she arrested her speech and started smiling, she answered that she was not able to speak anymore, and she was not able to explain the reason why she smiled.>

sites.effect: <Burst of laugh. Electrical stimulation elicited a smile, starting from the contralateral zygomaticus and the orbicularis oculi muscles, then involving the entire face, and eventually producing laugh. Also in this case the patient felt amused and reported that he could not restrain from laughing. The effect of the stimulation was not restricted to the production of a facial expression, but also elicited a clear feeling of mirth. More specifically, patient arrested the reading asked by the neurologist, and started to laugh. Patient 1 attributed their reaction to the impulse to laugh, without knowing the reason why. sites.effect: <Laugh without mirth. The electrical stimulation elicited a smile starting from the contralateral side of the face, but without mirth. During the elicited expression patients continued to read. At the end of the stimulation Patient 6 spontaneously said that he could not keep from smiling, and reported a sensation diffused to the contralateral part of the face, as well as the feeling that the cheek was lifted. Interestingly, Patient 6 reported sensations not involving the facial muscles, i.e., a shiver to the stomach, to the throat, or to the whole body>

sites.effect: Alexia - <P1 was unable to execute written commands, but executed the same commands promptly if they were given orally during the stimulation. Writing sentences to dictation was performed with ease, but he was unable to read those sentences when they were presented to him visually during a subsequent stimulation in random order, after intervening distractor tasks. These findings were consistent with pure alexia without agraphia. At electrode SC3, P1 was able to name pictures but unable to follow written commands. >

sites.effect: Alexia - <P1 was unable to execute written commands, but executed the same commands promptly if they were given orally during the stimulation. sites.effect: Alexia - <Stimulation of electrode SC9 replicated the findings seen at SC3 of patient P1. On more detailed testing of reading, P2 was able to read letters but could not read words or sentences. P2 read short words (three to four letters) by spelling them out aloud letter by letter. Reading and comprehension of single and multidigit numbers and picture naming were intact. He was able to perform simple oral and written arithmetic. Writing to dictation was intact for complicated words and sentences, consistent with alexia without agraphia. Copying was slower with a few errors>

sites.effect: Alexia - <Arrest of reading was noted, with marked difficulty in reading comprehension. Spontaneous speech, auditory comprehension, and writing (spontaneously and to dictation) were intact. P3 was unable to read sentences and words. Letter by letter reading was performed with a few mistakes. He read out “finger” as “f . . . a . . . n . . . g . . . e . . . l” and pronounced it true to the letters as “fangel.” He read “close” as “c . . . l . . . a . . . s . . . e” and pronounced it accordingly. Spelling of words given orally during the stimulation was prompt and correct. Picture naming was impaired. To the picture of a chair he responded “sit down.” On seeing a hammer, he mimicked its use with his hand but was unable to name it. P3 was able to read numbers and perform simple oral and written calculations. However, he was unable to read a number when it was written in words.>
